children: New Delhi, Nov. 17 -- Cleaning up business operations by cutting emissions and adopting more sustainable practices is not a political choice but a future-driven economic one, said Jesper Brodin, chair of the Earthshot Prize and former chief executive of Ingka Group, which runs most IKEA stores.

The prize was established in 2020 by Britain's Prince William to recognize innovative solutions to major environmental challenges. Each winner receives £1 million, about 12.3 crore based on Tuesday's exchange rate.

In a virtual interview with Mint from the Earthshot Prize 2026 venue in Mumbai, Brodin said policymakers and businesses around the world can "do better" on emissions because reducing them goes beyond any political debate.
"This is about things bigger than political goals or profits. This is about saving the planet, a very existential challenge," he said.

"Cleaner business operations are not a political choice, but a futuristic one and certainly an economic one. In most cases, and even in hard-to-abate sectors, you will find that strategies to reduce emissions are actually economically more viable," said Brodin, who is in India as chair of the Board of Trustees of the Earthshot Prize, a role he took up in March.
Hard-to-abate sectors include steel, cement and mining, among others, where high energy demand, process emissions, and limited low-carbon alternatives make decarbonization challenging.

"Take the example of Ørsted. 20 years ago, they were one of Europe's most coal-intensive utilities and then made the decision to rebuild their business around renewable energy and cut their direct carbon emissions by more than 98%," he said.

Denmark-based Ørsted, earlier an oil and gas explorer and coal-based electricity generator, is now one of the world's largest developers of offshore wind farms. The Danish state-controlled energy company is among the finalists for this year's Earthshot Prize.

Brodin, in his 2017-2025 stint as Ingka Group CEO, was responsible for reducing emissions of the Swedish mass-market furniture retailer. In a March 2026 interview with TIME magazine, he said IKEA's transition to renewable energy was almost complete, and remarked that IKEA "has become a medium-sized utility company today".

The Ingka Group had invested €4.3 billion in renewable energy generation and storage by March 2026, its website said. These investments were in wind and solar energy projects as well as energy storage projects.

The Ingka Group said that it develops, constructs, acquires and operates utility-scale wind, solar and storage projects and sells renewable energy to reduce the climate footprint of the Group and the IKEA value chain.

Brodin's views come at a time when geoeconomic fragmentation is dominating global policymaking, and global disruptions and uncertainties such as trade barriers and tariffs, as well as wars, are ongoing.

A May 2026 research report by World Bank economists Phil Levy and Achim Vogt noted that trade policy fragmentation has increased over time since the formation of the World Trade Organisation in 1995, meaning that "countries are increasingly applying different tariffs to different partners for the same product".
"The rise in trade policy fragmentation allows countries to change policies quickly. In recent years, this has been accompanied by a rise in trade policy uncertainty," the report said.

At this time, India, the world's most populous country with approximately 1.4 billion people, is also the world's third-largest energy consumer and one of the world's largest crude oil importers, relying on imports for nearly 90% of its crude oil requirements.

"India has thousands of years of traditions and culture, and at the same time, thousands of years of business experience also. What we need to understand here is that the past and the future are not enemies. India should move ahead and make future-driven economic choices while also retaining the thousands of years of tradition and culture that are indigenous to it," said Brodin.
He also said India had taken great strides in electric mobility, citing vehicles built by homegrown automaker Mahindra & Mahindra, another finalist in the 2026 Earthshot Awards.
Mint's queries emailed to Mahindra & Mahindra and Ørsted on Monday evening remained unanswered.
"Sustainable practices are a clear economic choice. You can see the transition benefiting businesses everywhere, and that is why something like electric mobility is here to stay," he said.

Businesses worldwide require predictable policy environments to operate, he said. "Global disruptions affect businesses, and questions about investment have to be raised. It is a global investment dampener," said Brodin, speaking about continuous geopolitical disruptions over the last few years, including a pandemic, tariff tussles, and multiple wars.

"There are three things that businesses want from governments. One, a predictable policy environment within the country. Two, smooth cross-border operations, and three, continuous involvement in dialogue for new policies," he said.
"We must understand that businesses are builders, and it is a gradual process. So, sudden shifts can only impact a business adversely," he said.

title: Going green is not politics, it's economics: Jesper Brodin, chair of the Earthshot Prize
